Instructions: A pathogen and clinical setting is named, with multiple
approved or late-stage investigational antibacterials in the candidate set.
Rank the candidates by net clinical effectiveness considering activity
vs the pathogen, safety, practicality (route, frequency, monitoring),
resistance evolution risk, and stewardship cost. Justify the ranking
position by position with reference to specific drug features and
cite the trial / guideline that supports the conclusion.

Triage scenario: Severe Candida glabrata candidemia — rank micafungin vs caspofungin vs liposomal amphotericin B
response:
Setting: ICU patient with C. glabrata candidemia, no FKS-mutation
data yet (FKS sequencing pending), creatinine 1.4. Ranking. (1)
Micafungin 100 mg IV q24h — first-line per IDSA candidiasis 2016.
Reasons: (a) echinocandin glucan-synthase inhibitor with fungicidal
activity against most C. glabrata; (b) MIC50 0.06 ug/mL; (c) no
renal dose adjustment (hepatic clearance); (d) once-daily simple
dosing; (e) lower hepatic enzyme rise than caspofungin in some
registry data. Trade-offs: 8 to 12 percent FKS-mutant prevalence in
tertiary centers — repeat MIC essential, switch if rising. (2)
Caspofungin 70 mg IV load then 50 mg q24h — equivalent first-line
choice. Reasons: same echinocandin mechanism; well-validated trial
data (Mora-Duarte 2002 NEJM); slightly different metabolism. Trade-offs:
hepatic enzyme rise 5 to 10 percent (vs micafungin's lower); caspofungin
Child-Pugh B requires dose reduction to 35 mg q24h. The clinical
preference between micafungin and caspofungin is institution-driven.
(3) Liposomal amphotericin B 3 to 4 mg/kg IV q24h — second-line
reserved for echinocandin-intolerant or echinocandin-resistant
(FKS-mutant) C. glabrata. Reasons: ergosterol pore mechanism is
orthogonal to echinocandin glucan-synthase target — no cross-resistance
to FKS mutations. Trade-offs: nephrotoxicity even with liposomal
formulation (5 to 10 percent), potassium and magnesium wasting,
infusion reactions; clinical efficacy somewhat lower against
C. glabrata than echinocandins. Net: echinocandin (micafungin or
caspofungin) > liposomal AmphoB for first-line C. glabrata candidemia.

Instructions: Propose specific structural modifications to the named drug to defeat the named resistance mechanism. Provide the modified SMILES (or describe the modification precisely), explain why it should work, predict the new MIC range, and identify likely trade-offs.
Drug: Meropenem
Resistance: OXA-23 carbapenemase (Class D, dominant in CRAB — carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii; +/- CarO porin loss)
Question: Design a meropenem variant active on OXA-23+ CRAB.
response:
PROBLEM: OXA-23 (Class D serine β-lactamase) is the dominant carbapenemase in CRAB. AVIBACTAM + VABORBACTAM + RELEBACTAM all have LIMITED OXA-23 activity. DURLOBACTAM (in Xacduro 2023) is the first BLI with strong OXA-23 inhibition. Combined with CarO porin loss + AdeABC efflux, CRAB is among the hardest pathogens to treat.

DESIGN STRATEGY — multiple parallel approaches.

Strategy A — PAIR MEROPENEM WITH DURLOBACTAM. Sulbactam-durlobactam (Xacduro) covers CRAB. Add MEROPENEM for additional PBP coverage (durlobactam protects from OXA-23). Triple combo: MEROPENEM + SULBACTAM + DURLOBACTAM.

Strategy B — SIDEROPHORE-CARBAPENEM CONJUGATE (cefiderocol-style). Replace meropenem's C3-carboxyl with CATECHOL siderophore. Bypasses CarO porin loss + provides MBL stability.

Strategy C — MODIFY MEROPENEM C2 SUBSTITUENT to better resist OXA-23. The 1-β-methyl + (S)-N-METHYL-PYRROLIDINYL-CARBOXAMIDE-THIO C2 of meropenem is moderately recognized by OXA-23. Replace with a BULKIER + MORE RIGID C2 (e.g., spirocyclic bicyclic amine) → harder for OXA-23 to acylate.

Strategy D — PAIR WITH POLYMYXIN for synergy (covered in Sprint 4 synergy). Polymyxin permeabilizes outer membrane → meropenem reaches PBPs faster than OXA-23 hydrolyzes.

PROPOSAL — 'MERO-CRAB-1' (Strategy A + C combined):
Modified meropenem with bicyclic C2 substituent + paired with sulbactam-durlobactam.

PREDICTED OUTCOME: MIC vs OXA-23+ CRAB = 4-8 µg/mL (vs meropenem >32 µg/mL on same strain). Meaningful coverage for CRAB.

TRADE-OFFS: Triple-component therapy (meropenem + sulbactam + durlobactam) = more complex IV infusion. Cost ~$3-5K/day. Reserved for severe CRAB infections only.

VALIDATION: OXA-23 enzyme kinetics vs all variants + isogenic CarO+/CarO- + AdeABC+/- strains.

prompt:
Instructions: A specific structural feature of an existing antimicrobial is
hypothetically removed or substituted. Reason through (1) the role that
feature plays in target binding or PK, (2) the predicted MIC shift across
representative pathogens, (3) whether resistance mechanisms change, (4) the
PK or toxicity consequence, (5) the medicinal-chemistry lesson — what the
feature is "buying" the molecule.

Counterfactual: Remove the 1-beta-methyl group from meropenem
response:
The 1-beta-methyl on the carbapenem ring of meropenem sterically blocks
renal dehydropeptidase-1 (DHP-1) from accessing the C1 position; this
is the SAR feature that distinguishes meropenem (DHP-stable, no cilastatin
needed) from imipenem (no 1-substituent, requires 1:1 cilastatin co-administration
to retain urinary recovery). Removing the 1-beta-methyl reverts meropenem
to thienamycin-style DHP vulnerability: predicted urinary recovery would
drop from around 70 percent to less than 20 percent without cilastatin,
requiring partner-drug co-administration to be clinically usable. Antibacterial
MICs would NOT change (1-beta-methyl is a PK feature, not a target-binding
feature for PBP1a/2/3 of E. coli, K. pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa). Resistance
to KPC, NDM, OXA-48 carbapenemases would remain identical because hydrolysis
acts on the C2-C3 beta-lactam carbonyl, distant from C1. Toxicity would also
shift: the 1-beta-methyl reduces GABA-A receptor binding affinity at high
CSF concentrations (imipenem-cilastatin has 1 to 3 percent seizure rate at
meningitis doses; meropenem under 0.5 percent). Removing the methyl would
raise seizure risk to imipenem level, restricting CNS dosing. Lesson: the
1-beta-methyl is one of the highest-leverage single SAR moves in the
carbapenem class — it removed the partner drug requirement AND lowered
neurotoxicity simultaneously. Ertapenem and doripenem also carry the
1-beta-methyl for the same reason.

feature is "buying" the molecule.

Counterfactual: Remove the C2-amidine of meropenem (carbapenem ring)
response:
Carbapenems share a bicyclic beta-lactam-pyrrolidine core; meropenem,
imipenem, ertapenem, and doripenem all carry a C2 amidine substituent
(a pyrrolidine carboxamide in meropenem's case, with various extensions).
The C2-amidine reaches into the active-site channel of PBP1a, PBP2, and
PBP3 of Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas, providing the "second-pocket"
contact that boosts affinity by 100-fold over a bare carbapenem
scaffold. The amidine also stabilizes the carbapenem ring against
hydrolysis by class A serine carbapenemases via electrostatic
interaction with active-site residues. Remove the C2-amidine (replace
with hydrogen or methyl, yielding the parent carbapenem-3-carboxylic
acid scaffold): predicted MIC against E. coli rises from 0.06 to 4 to 8;
against P. aeruginosa from 0.5 to greater than 32; against MSSA from
0.06 to 2 to 4. Anaerobic activity (B. fragilis) collapses too. Resistance
to KPC, NDM, OXA-48 carbapenemases is unchanged in pattern but the drug
is already clinically inactive. PK consequence: the C2-amidine is also
the metabolic handle for renal organic-anion-transporter (OAT) secretion;
its removal would alter renal clearance kinetics. Toxicity: C2 amidine
contributes to the GABA-receptor binding affinity that drives carbapenem
seizures (especially imipenem); removing it might reduce CNS toxicity
paradoxically while eliminating antibacterial activity. Lesson: the C2
substituent is the "antibiotic engine" of the carbapenem class —
every member retains it (with class-distinguishing modifications). The
carbapenem ring alone is necessary but not sufficient; class-defining
activity requires C2 elaboration.

Instructions: Propose specific structural modifications to the named drug to defeat the named resistance mechanism. Provide the modified SMILES (or describe the modification precisely), explain why it should work, predict the new MIC range, and identify likely trade-offs.
Drug: Isoniazid (INH)
Resistance mechanism: katG Ser315Thr mutation (the most common INH-resistance mutation in clinical Mtb; ~50× MIC shift; reduces katG-mediated INH activation)
Question: Design an INH variant that retains activity on katG-deficient or katG-mutant Mtb strains.
response:
PROBLEM ANALYSIS. INH is a PRODRUG activated by Mtb's CATALASE-PEROXIDASE enzyme katG. KatG oxidizes INH to an isonicotinoyl-acyl radical, which then forms a covalent adduct with NAD/NADP cofactor — the active INH-NAD ADDUCT inhibits InhA (the FAS-II enoyl-ACP reductase essential for mycolic acid synthesis). KatG mutations (especially Ser315Thr) DEACTIVATE the prodrug → no active warhead → 50-100× MIC shift.

DESIGN APPROACHES — BYPASS katG-MEDIATED ACTIVATION OR USE ALTERNATIVE ACTIVATION.

STRATEGY 1: PRE-FORMED INH-NAD ADDUCT.
Synthesize the INH-NAD adduct chemically + administer directly. NAD's pyridine + INH's pyridine form a STABLE C-C bond after katG-mediated radical addition. Synthesis is feasible (Tonge et al.). PROBLEMS: (a) INH-NAD adduct is HIGHLY POLAR (NAD-derived) → no oral bioavailability, (b) IV administration challenging (size + complex formulation), (c) cell membrane uptake limited.

STRATEGY 2: ALTERNATIVE PRODRUG ACTIVATION VIA mShAA (mycothiol amide hydrolase) OR EthA.
Design a NEW INH-LIKE PRODRUG that uses a DIFFERENT Mtb activator. ETHIONAMIDE (a well-known TB drug) is activated by EthA (mono-oxygenase), bypasses katG entirely. Cross-resistance to INH-katG mutants is MINIMAL.
PROPOSAL: ETHIONAMIDE-INH HYBRID — combine EthA-activatable thiocarbamate + InhA-inhibiting isonicotinoyl warhead. After EthA oxidation, releases isonicotinoyl-NAD adduct that inhibits InhA. Bypasses katG but engages same target.

STRATEGY 3: DIRECT InhA INHIBITION (not requiring katG activation).
DESIGN A MOLECULE THAT BINDS InhA DIRECTLY without prodrug activation — no katG dependency. Several research-stage InhA inhibitors exist:
  - PT70 (4-amino-pyrimidine series, Tonge lab)
  - 'Direct InhA inhibitors' from Sequella, Novartis, AstraZeneca
PROPOSAL: develop an InhA-PROXIMAL pharmacophore — e.g., a TRICLOSAN-LIKE NA Reductase inhibitor (triclosan inhibits InhA in vitro) BUT with optimized Mtb selectivity (avoid mammalian fatty acid synthase off-target).

STRATEGY 4: INH WITH METAL CHELATION TO SELF-OXIDIZE.
Design INH with INTRINSIC OXIDATION CAPACITY — e.g., INH conjugated to a Fe(III)-chelator that, in the Mtb cytoplasm, GENERATES INH RADICAL CHEMISTRY VIA Fe-CATALYZED FENTON-LIKE REACTION (no katG required). Conceptually clean but pharmacologically challenging.

RECOMMENDED PROPOSAL: 'INH-EthA-ESCAPE' (Strategy 2 hybrid).
Structure: thiocarbamate-isonicotinoyl prodrug:
  S=C(NH-CH3)-NH-S(O2)-CH2-C(=O)-NH-NH2 + isonicotinoyl moiety appended
Modified SMILES (proof of concept): NN=C(N)c1ccncc1.S(=O)(=O)(NC(=S)N(C)C)CCC(=O)O
(precise structure designed iteratively to optimize EthA hydrolysis kinetics)
PREDICTED OUTCOME on katG Ser315Thr mutant Mtb: MIC 1-4 µg/mL (vs INH 32-64 µg/mL on same strain). Cross-resistance to ETHIONAMIDE-resistant strains (with ethA mutations) is a concern but ETH resistance is much rarer than katG resistance.

TRADE-OFFS. (1) ETH-class hepatotoxicity (well-documented). (2) ETH's GI side effects (nausea, vomiting). (3) Potential cross-resistance to ETH itself (ethA mutations).

STRATEGY 5 (BACKUP): SIMPLY USE EXISTING ETHIONAMIDE.
ETHIONAMIDE is FDA-approved + WHO Group C TB drug. For katG-mutant Mtb (INH-resistant), ethionamide is the standard alternative. Doesn't require new chemistry — just better stewardship.

VALIDATION PATH. (1) Synthesize INH-EthA-Escape candidate. (2) MIC vs WT Mtb + katG-Ser315Thr mutant + ethA mutant + multi-drug-resistant clinical isolates. (3) Hepatotoxicity in mouse + dog models. (4) PK studies. (5) Phase I in healthy volunteers. (6) Phase II in MDR-TB patients.

PK or toxicity consequence, (5) the medicinal-chemistry lesson — what the

Counterfactual: Remove the para-aminobenzoic-acid mimicry from sulfamethoxazole
response:
Sulfamethoxazole's antibacterial activity arises from its mimicry of
para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), the natural substrate of bacterial
dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS). The 4-amino group on the phenyl ring of
sulfamethoxazole is critical — it occupies the PABA-recognition pocket of
DHPS at residues Arg63, Arg255, Asp184 (E. coli numbering), and the
sulfonamide group mimics PABA's carboxylate. Replace the 4-amino with
hydrogen (becoming a generic phenyl-sulfonamide without the amine handle):
DHPS no longer recognizes the molecule because the H-bond donor at the
4-position is gone, and the sulfonamide alone has no DHPS binding affinity.
Predicted MIC against susceptible E. coli rises from 1 to 4 ug/mL
(sulfamethoxazole) to greater than 128 (effectively inactive); same for
Stenotrophomonas, Listeria, PCP. Resistance mechanisms become irrelevant
(sul1, sul2 still mediate bacterial DHPS sub-pocket changes that hit any
sulfa-PABA mimic, but base-line activity is lost). Mammalian cells lack
DHPS (we acquire folate from diet) so removing the amine doesn't change
mammalian selectivity, just abolishes antibacterial activity entirely.
PK shift: 4-amino is the metabolic handle for N-acetylation (the cause
of sulfa hypersensitivity in slow-acetylator phenotypes). Removing it
eliminates that toxicity arc but also removes the drug. Lesson: the
4-amino is the entire pharmacophore of the sulfa class — every sulfonamide
antibiotic from sulfanilamide (1935) to sulfamethoxazole (1960s) retains it.

Drug class: Carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem)
Pathogens: MSSA, MRSA, VRE, KPC-CRE, NDM-CRE, OXA-48 CRE, MDR P. aeruginosa, OXA-23 CRAB, B. fragilis, Mtb
Question: Map carbapenem coverage across MDR pathogens — explain which carbapenemases defeat them and the modern BLI rescues.

Carbapenem spectrum across MDR pathogens — the CRITICAL clinical map:

**MSSA** (MIC 0.06-0.5 µg/mL, EFFECTIVE):
Carbapenems (especially meropenem) bind PBP1, 2, 3 of S. aureus with high affinity. MSSA is carbapenem-susceptible. Used as broad-spectrum empirical Rx + when MSSA is part of a polymicrobial infection.

**MRSA** (MIC 8-32 µg/mL, RESISTANT):
MRSA's mecA-encoded PBP2a has 1000× LOWER AFFINITY for ALL classical β-lactams INCLUDING CARBAPENEMS. Carbapenems do NOT engage PBP2a. NEED: ceftaroline or ceftobiprole (anti-MRSA cephalosporins) or vancomycin/daptomycin/linezolid.

**VRE** (MIC ≥64 µg/mL, INTRINSIC RESISTANCE):
Enterococcal PBP5fm has CONSTITUTIVELY LOW affinity for cephalosporins + carbapenems. Intrinsic carbapenem resistance regardless of vanA. Use linezolid/daptomycin/ampicillin (E. faecalis) instead.

**KPC-CRE** (MIC 4-128 µg/mL, RESISTANT):
KPC carbapenemase (Class A serine β-lactamase, dominant in US/Europe) hydrolyzes carbapenems. RESCUE: meropenem-VABORBACTAM (Vabomere 2017) or ceftazidime-AVIBACTAM (Avycaz 2015) or imipenem-RELEBACTAM (Recarbrio 2019) — all 3 BLI partners restore activity.

**NDM-CRE** (MIC ≥128 µg/mL, RESISTANT):
NDM Class B Zn-dependent metallo-β-lactamase hydrolyzes carbapenems. NO BLI in current clinical use inhibits MBLs (vaborbactam, avibactam, relebactam, durlobactam ALL inactive on MBLs). RESCUE: AZTREONAM-AVIBACTAM (Emblaveo 2024 EU) — aztreonam is MBL-stable + avibactam covers co-produced ESBL/AmpC. CEFIDEROCOL (Fetroja 2019) also active vs NDM. TANIBORBACTAM (Phase III) is the FIRST clinical MBL-active BLI in development.

**OXA-48 CRE** (MIC 4-32 µg/mL, INTERMEDIATE-RESISTANT):
OXA-48 (Class D) hydrolyzes carbapenems AT MODERATE EFFICIENCY (slower than KPC). Often porin loss + OXA-48 combination is needed for full clinical resistance. RESCUE: ceftazidime-avibactam (Avycaz) — avibactam inhibits OXA-48 efficiently.

**MDR P. aeruginosa** (MIC variable, often RESISTANT):
Paer can use multiple resistance mechanisms: chromosomal AmpC (PDC) hyperproduction + OprD porin loss + MexAB-OprM efflux. Modern Paer strains often have 2-3 of these → carbapenem-resistant. RESCUE: ceftolozane-tazobactam (Zerbaxa 2014), imipenem-relebactam (Recarbrio), cefiderocol.

**OXA-23 CRAB (carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter)** (MIC ≥32 µg/mL, RESISTANT):
OXA-23 (Class D Acinetobacter) + Carbapenem resistance + porin loss (CarO) + AdeABC efflux. Among the HARDEST to treat. RESCUE: SULBACTAM-DURLOBACTAM (Xacduro 2023, FIRST anti-CRAB drug) or CEFIDEROCOL or polymyxin combinations.

**B. fragilis** (MIC 0.06-0.5 µg/mL, EFFECTIVE):
Carbapenems are FIRST-LINE for B. fragilis (and broadly for anaerobic infections). Excellent anaerobic coverage. Often used in intra-abdominal infection empirical therapy.

**M. tuberculosis** (MIC 1-4 µg/mL, MODERATE):
Mtb has L,D-transpeptidases (LDTs) that carbapenems can engage at MODERATE affinity. Used in MDR-TB salvage regimens (typically as part of meropenem-clavulanate combination, where clavulanate inhibits Mtb's BlaC β-lactamase that would otherwise destroy meropenem). NICHE use.

**SUMMARY FRAMEWORK**:
Carbapenem spectrum determined by PBP affinity + carbapenemase status:
1. WT bacteria with high PBP affinity → SUSCEPTIBLE.
2. mecA (MRSA) PBP2a → INTRINSIC RESISTANCE (need ceftaroline/ceftobiprole).
3. Enterococcal PBP5fm → INTRINSIC RESISTANCE.
4. CARBAPENEMASE PRODUCTION (KPC, OXA, NDM, VIM, IMP, OXA-48) → ACQUIRED RESISTANCE.
5. Modern BLIs: vaborbactam/avibactam/relebactam/durlobactam — each covers different    carbapenemase classes. NDM remains the OPEN PROBLEM (only ATM-AVI + cefiderocol + emerging    taniborbactam).

Instructions: Design a novel drug to meet the specified criteria. Propose a structural outline, explain the design rationale, predict potency + safety, identify trade-offs, and describe a validation path.
Target profile: Oral activity vs CRE Enterobacterales (E. coli, Klebsiella) for outpatient management of complicated UTI
Design criteria: Oral bioavailability >50%; MIC ≤2 µg/mL on KPC-CRE Enterobacterales; resistance to CYP3A4 metabolism; once-daily dosing; minimal hepatic toxicity
Question: Design an oral antibiotic that retains activity against CRE Enterobacterales for outpatient cUTI management.
response:
DESIGN PROBLEM SUMMARY.
Currently, MOST anti-CRE drugs are IV ONLY (ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam, sulbactam-durlobactam, cefiderocol). The only ORAL options for CRE cUTI are: nitrofurantoin (if susceptible), fosfomycin (single oral dose), ertapenem IM/IV (not oral). NEED: TRUE ORAL ANTI-CRE drug for outpatient management. This would enable TRANSITION-of-CARE from inpatient IV to outpatient oral, reducing hospital stays + costs.

DESIGN STRATEGY — Three parallel approaches.

**APPROACH 1: ORAL NBTI (gepotidacin-class, but more potent on CRE).**
GEPOTIDACIN (Blujepa, FDA 2025) is the FIRST oral NBTI — already covers WT Enterobacterales but MIC on CRE-Kp is moderate (1-8 µg/mL). DESIGN A NEXT-GEN NBTI with:
  - Modified GyrB binding pocket affinity for CRE-specific GyrB variants
  - REDUCED EFFLUX SUSCEPTIBILITY (AcrAB-TolC + KP-specific RamA)
  - MAINTAINED ORAL bioavailability (>50%)
Specific structural proposal: TRIAZAACENAPHTHYLENE scaffold with:
  - 4-FLUORINATED phenyl extension (vs gepotidacin's unsubstituted) for additional GyrB pocket     H-bonding
  - PEG-amide tail for increased polarity (improved solubility + reduced AcrAB recognition)
  - Smaller MW <450 to retain oral absorption
PREDICTED MIC vs KPC-CRE: 0.5-2 µg/mL (vs gepotidacin 1-4 µg/mL).

**APPROACH 2: ORAL β-LACTAM + ORAL AVIBACTAM.**
AVIBACTAM is currently IV-only. The challenge: avibactam is highly polar (DBO with sulfooxy + carboxamide). DESIGN AN ORAL AVIBACTAM PRODRUG:

Drug: Nitrofurantoin
response:
Synthetic 5-nitrofuran — small molecule (238 Da) — prodrug requiring

reduction), so nitrofurantoin works against aerobic bacteria. Selectivity:
mammalian cells reduce nitrofurantoin much less efficiently than
bacteria, providing an antibacterial-selective window. Spectrum:
gram-positive (S. saprophyticus, Enterococcus including some VRE,
MSSA partially, Group B streptococcus), gram-negative (E. coli,
Klebsiella, Citrobacter, Enterobacter — variable), urinary pathogens.
Inactive against Proteus, Providencia, Serratia (intrinsic), Pseudomonas,

narrow-spectrum, avoids fluoroquinolone collateral); AVOID for
pyelonephritis (insufficient renal-tissue concentration), prostatitis
(poor prostate penetration), or any non-urinary indication.

Question: Walk through meropenem's complete mechanism: the 1β-METHYL modification that gave DHP-1 stability, broad PBP affinity, the β-lactamase resistance hierarchy, KPC-mediated CRE breakthrough + meropenem-vaborbactam (Vabomere) rescue, and modern positioning vs imipenem and ertapenem.
response:
Drug profile. MEROPENEM (Sumitomo SM-7338, marketed by Pfizer/AstraZeneca as MERREM/MERONEM, FDA 1996) — the SECOND-GENERATION CARBAPENEM and modern WORKHORSE for serious gram-negative + mixed infections. Replaced imipenem-cilastatin in many empiric regimens due to better safety + no need for cilastatin. Generic since ~2010.

STRUCTURAL DESIGN — IMIPENEM EVOLVED.
(1) CARBAPENEM CORE — β-lactam fused to cyclopentenyl (5-ring with C-C-C-C-C pyrroline + Δ2     unsaturation), C2-C3 double bond, C3-COOH.
(2) (R)-1-HYDROXYETHYL at C6 — the carbapenem stereo-defining feature, blocks β-lactamase     deacylation by sterically interfering with the catalytic water.
(3) **1β-METHYL at C1** — THE KEY MEROPENEM INNOVATION (vs imipenem which has 1-H). The methyl     group at C1 (β-face) provides STERIC PROTECTION against renal DEHYDROPEPTIDASE-1 (DHP-1) —     DHP-1 hydrolyzes carbapenems in renal proximal tubule. Imipenem requires CILASTATIN co-    administration to block DHP-1; MEROPENEM IS DHP-1-STABLE → no cilastatin needed.
(4) C2 substituent = (S)-N-METHYL-PYRROLIDINE-2-CARBOXAMIDE-CARBONYL-THIO — pyrrolidine bearing     a (S)-stereo carbon with N,N-dimethyl-aminocarbonyl. Provides good gram-neg porin permeation     + binding affinity to PBPs.
(5) Net charge: zwitterionic at pH 7.4 (β-lactam C3-COO⁻ + pyrrolidine N+ at C2 substituent).

TARGET — BROAD PBP COVERAGE.
Meropenem binds with high affinity (Ki nM-low µM range) to virtually ALL essential bacterial PBPs across species:
    E. coli: PBP1a + PBP1b + PBP2 + PBP3 — covers cell wall + division + shape
    P. aeruginosa: PBP1 + PBP2 + PBP3 — strong anti-Paer activity
    S. aureus: PBP1 + PBP2 + PBP3 (NOT PBP2a — see resistance below)
    Anaerobes (B. fragilis): high affinity
BACTERICIDAL kinetics, time-dependent. PK/PD predictor: T>MIC ≥ 40-50% of dosing interval (less stringent than for cephalosporins because of carbapenem's slower deacylation = longer effective PBP block).

MECHANISM OF β-LACTAMASE STABILITY.
Carbapenems are stable against most CLASS A (TEM, SHV, CTX-M ESBLs), CLASS C (AmpC) β-lactamases due to the (R)-1-HYDROXYETHYL group at C6. The 1β-methyl additionally blocks DHP-1.
BUT: SPECIFIC CARBAPENEMASES exist:
  CLASS A: KPC (KPC-2/3 dominant, US/Europe) — major CRE driver
  CLASS B (METALLO): NDM (Indian subcontinent), VIM (EU), IMP (Asia/Pacific) — Zn²⁺-dependent
  CLASS D: OXA-48 (Mediterranean/Middle East), OXA-23/24/40 (Acinetobacter)
These hydrolyze meropenem efficiently → CARBAPENEM-RESISTANT ENTEROBACTERALES (CRE) etc.

MEROPENEM-VABORBACTAM (VABOMERE) — THE KPC-CRE RESCUE.
Vaborbactam (RPX7009) — a CYCLIC BORONATE β-lactamase inhibitor (different scaffold from diazabicyclooctanes like avibactam). Specifically inhibits CLASS A β-lactamases (KPC, ESBLs). Does NOT inhibit class B (MBLs) or class D (OXAs). Combined with meropenem (Vabomere, FDA 2017) for KPC-CRE infections (cUTI primarily). Standard dose: 4 g IV q8h (2 g meropenem + 2 g vaborbactam). Alternative to ceftazidime-avibactam for KPC-CRE.

SPECTRUM. (a) ENTEROBACTERALES: EXCELLENT (E. coli, K. pneumoniae, Enterobacter, Citrobacter, Serratia, Proteus all MIC 0.03-0.5 µg/mL on WT). (b) PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA: GOOD on WT (MIC 0.5-2 µg/mL); resistance via OprD porin loss + AmpC + MexAB efflux is common in clinical isolates. (c) ACINETOBACTER: variable on WT, RESISTANT in CRAB (OXA-23). (d) GRAM-POS: GOOD on Streptococci, MSSA, Enterococcus faecalis (E. faecium intrinsic resistance). MRSA: NEGLIGIBLE (no PBP2a engagement). (e) ANAEROBES: EXCELLENT (B. fragilis, Clostridium). (f) ATYPICALS: weak.

PHARMACOKINETICS. (1) IV only. (2) Standard dose 1 g IV q8h, can extend to 2 g q8h for severe infection or Pseudomonas. (3) PROLONGED INFUSION (3-hour) improves T>MIC for resistant isolates. (4) Half-life ~1 hour (renal elimination). Dose-adjust for CrCl <50. (5) GOOD CSF PENETRATION (unlike imipenem which is more variable) — meropenem is FIRST-LINE for bacterial meningitis due to gram-negs / Listeria / Pseudomonas. (6) Lung penetration ~25-50% serum.

ADVERSE EFFECTS. (1) HYPERSENSITIVITY (cross-reactive with penicillin allergy ~5-10% rate, lower than for direct penicillin re-exposure). (2) C. difficile colitis (any β-lactam). (3) SEIZURE risk lower than imipenem (imipenem has GABA-A antagonism via N-formimidoyl side chain; meropenem's pyrrolidinyl C2 has lower GABA-A affinity). Still, neurological adverse events possible at high doses + renal impairment. (4) Hepatic transaminase elevation. (5) Eosinophilia.

(1) CARBAPENEMASES (KPC, NDM, VIM, OXA-48, OXA-23) — primary resistance.
(2) PORIN LOSS (OmpK35/OmpK36 in Klebsiella; OprD in Pseudomonas) — synergizes with weak β-lactamases. CrtP loss in Enterobacter.
(3) AmpC HYPERPRODUCTION + porin loss = clinical resistance.
(4) Efflux upregulation (Paer MexAB-OprM) — modest.
(5) PBP3 mutations — rare, modest effect.

Drug: Trimethoprim
response:
Synthetic 2,4-diaminopyrimidine, structural analog of dihydrofolate.
Chemistry: 2,4-diaminopyrimidine ring (the substrate-mimicking head)
linked via a methylene bridge to a 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenyl ring (the
hydrophobic anchor). The 2,4-diamino group hydrogen-bonds with bacterial
DHFR active-site residues (Glu30, Asp27 in E. coli numbering),
mimicking the hydrogen-bond pattern of dihydrofolate's pteridine ring.
Mechanism: competitively inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase
(DHFR), the enzyme that reduces dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate
using NADPH. Tetrahydrofolate is the universal carrier of
one-carbon units for thymidine, purine, methionine, and serine
synthesis; blocking DHFR halts thymidine production and stops DNA
replication. Selectivity: bacterial DHFR has different active-site
geometry than mammalian DHFR — trimethoprim has 60,000-fold higher
affinity for bacterial DHFR than human DHFR. Single-agent action is
bacteriostatic; combined with sulfamethoxazole (which blocks the
preceding DHPS step) becomes bactericidal via sequential pathway
blockade. Spectrum: broad — most Enterobacterales, S. aureus
(community MRSA), Stenotrophomonas, Burkholderia, Listeria, PCP,
Toxoplasma, Nocardia. Resistance: chromosomal DHFR mutations
(rarely clinically significant), or acquired dfrA17, dfrA1, dfrB
gene cassettes encoding plasmid-borne DHFR variants with reduced
TMP affinity (Ki 1000-fold higher), often in class 1 integrons
alongside sul1 (sulfonamide R), aac(6prime)-Ib-cr, and qnr. PK/PD:
AUC/MIC about 80 for combined TMP-SMX activity. Standard dose 160/800
mg PO BID (DS tab); 5 to 20 mg/kg/day TMP component IV for severe.
Tox: hyperkalemia (TMP blocks ENaC sodium channel in distal tubule,
same mechanism as amiloride), bone marrow suppression (folate-pathway
collateral on host hematopoiesis — give leucovorin if cytopenia),
hepatic enzyme rise, sulfa hypersensitivity (SJS/TEN at HLA-B*15:02
and B*58:01), nephrolithiasis (sulfamethoxazole crystallization).
Combination of TMP + sulfa is one of the most-used antibacterials
globally because of broad spectrum, oral availability, low cost.

response:

0.06 ug/mL (including ceftriaxone-R clinical isolates), S. aureus 1.

and confer 8 to 16-fold MIC rise; cross-resistance to FQ remains absent.

prolongation (~6 ms), no FDA black-box concerns. First oral antibiotic
with novel-target mechanism approved in over 20 years; positions for
drug-resistant gonorrhea (ceftriaxone-R) and FQ-R UTI.

80-year-old with fulminant C. difficile (toxic megacolon, septic shock,
ileus, lactate 5, WBC 28000) day 4 of fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID. Oral
vancomycin loaded as 500 mg PO/PR QID PLUS IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h
(the standard fulminant CDI regimen per IDSA-SHEA 2021 update). Rationale:
(1) ileus reduces gut transit so oral fidaxomicin or vancomycin alone
may not reach distal colon at therapeutic concentration; high-dose
vancomycin oral (500 mg QID instead of 125 mg) PLUS rectal vancomycin
retention enema (500 mg in 100 mL saline) to reach the colon
retrogradely; (2) IV metronidazole adds systemic-to-luminal penetration
(metronidazole concentrates in inflamed gut tissue). Vancomycin
oral binds C. difficile cell-wall D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of lipid II,
blocking transglycosylation; metronidazole prodrug is reduced by
C. difficile pyruvate-ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) to reactive
species that damage DNA. Resistance: rising metronidazole resistance in
C. difficile (5 to 15 percent in some surveillance, drove the IDSA
downgrade of metronidazole monotherapy from first-line); fidaxomicin
resistance via rpoB mutations rare but emerging. Surgical consultation
for emergency colectomy if hemodynamic deterioration despite medical
therapy (Sailhamer 2009 — colectomy reduces mortality 50 vs 90 percent
in fulminant CDI with peritonitis). Avoid: stopping fidaxomicin
prematurely if patient stabilizes; consider continuing fidaxomicin
AND adding vanco/metro for fulminant overlap. PK/PD: vanco oral
luminal AUC drives effect (no systemic level relevance for CDI);

Case: Linezolid for VRE bacteremia in thrombocytopenic patient — duration vs platelet floor
response:
(1) Susceptibility. CLSI linezolid breakpoint for Enterococcus is S ≤2, R ≥8
µg/mL. Most E. faecium VRE have MIC 1–2 — at the susceptibility edge. EUCAST

80–120 target. Standard 600 mg PO/IV q12h achieves AUC ~200; oral
bioavailability ~100%. Bacteriostatic activity is the key reason IDSA prefers

benefit), with linezolid as alternative. (3) Resistance. 23S rRNA G2576T
point mutation, cfr methyltransferase (also cross-resistant to phenicols /
lincosamides / streptogramin A / pleuromutilins — PhLOPSa pattern), optrA / poxtA
ribosomal protection on plasmids — emerging globally in livestock-linked VRE.

almost universal beyond 14 days; monitor CBC twice weekly. If platelets
<50 ×10⁹/L on therapy, switch to daptomycin 10 mg/kg q24h (if dapto-S). Other
tox: optic neuritis, peripheral neuropathy >28 d, lactic acidosis, serotonin
syndrome with SSRIs (MAO-A inhibition). (5) Alternatives. Daptomycin
(high-dose), tigecycline (only with combo, low serum levels — not preferred for
bacteremia), tedizolid (myelosuppression milder but limited enterococcal data),

Pathogen: Mycobacterium abscessus complex
response:
Resistance landscape: rapidly-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium

beta-lactamase hydrolyzes most beta-lactams; erm(41) gene confers

acid layer reduces drug penetration. The combined defenses make
M. abscessus complex among the most drug-resistant pathogens treated.
First-line (intensive phase, 4 to 6 weeks IV): amikacin 15 mg/kg IV
q24h PLUS imipenem 1 g IV q6h or cefoxitin 12 g/day IV PLUS azithromycin
500 mg PO daily (only if subsp. massiliense or erm(41) inactive subsp.
abscessus). Continuation phase (12 to 24 months oral): azithromycin +
clofazimine + linezolid + bedaquiline + tigecycline combinations
individualized. Clinical syndromes: chronic pulmonary infection
(especially in cystic fibrosis, structural lung disease,
bronchiectasis), skin/soft-tissue from contaminated water/aesthetic
procedures (tattoo, facial rejuvenation, breast implant, plastic
surgery), disseminated in immunocompromised. Diagnostics: AFB smear
and culture (rapidly growing, around 7 days vs M. tuberculosis 2 to
6 weeks); MALDI-TOF speciation; molecular subspecies identification

14-day incubation to detect inducible resistance). Stewardship/IC:
no person-to-person transmission for most cases (water/environmental
source); CF-specific transmissible clones with hyper-virulence

injection setups).

common in severe disease (TMP-SMX + meropenem, or TMP-SMX +
ceftazidime) for cystic fibrosis pulmonary exacerbation. Clinical
syndromes: chronic CF lung infection (B. cenocepacia is the most
virulent species and CONTRAINDICATES lung transplantation in many
programs because of high post-transplant mortality from B. cenocepacia

CURRENT TREATMENT (NO single best regimen).

ceiling around 0.6 ug/mL is the fundamental PK problem: tigecycline
distributes extensively into tissues (Vd 7 to 10 L/kg, lung-tissue

consistently — FDA 2010 black-box warning issued because pooled

glucuronidation clearance, lower dose 25 mg q12h after initial load.

Resistance determinant: gyrA/parC QRDR mutations (chromosomal fluoroquinolone-resistance)
response: Fluoroquinolones target DNA gyrase (gyrA + gyrB) and topoisomerase IV (parC + parE). GyrA α-helix and ParC analog form the quinolone-resistance-determining region (QRDR). Resistance mechanism: MmpS5-MmpL5 efflux in M. tuberculosis
response:
Molecular event: MmpS5 (mycobacterial membrane protein small 5) and MmpL5
(mycobacterial membrane protein large 5) form a two-component RND-family
efflux pump in M. tuberculosis. The pump is normally repressed by
Rv0678, a TetR-family transcriptional regulator. Mutations or insertions
in Rv0678 (loss-of-function) derepress mmpS5-mmpL5 transcription,
overexpressing the pump and increasing efflux of bedaquiline AND
clofazimine SIMULTANEOUSLY (cross-resistance phenotype). This is the
classic example of pre-existing low-level resistance creating a clinical
problem because of unsuspected cross-class effect. Bedaquiline binds
atpE c-ring of ATP synthase; clofazimine binds NADH dehydrogenase / has
multiple targets including phenazine-mediated reactive oxygen species.
The pump physically extrudes both drugs, raising their internal
concentrations only at high external concentrations. Importantly,
Rv0678 mutations emerge as PRE-existing low-frequency mutants in
treatment-naive M. tuberculosis populations (rate ~10^-8) and selected
under bedaquiline or clofazimine exposure. Distribution: chromosomal in
M. tuberculosis; rising with rollout of BPaL and BPaLM regimens for
MDR-TB. WHO surveillance reports emergent Rv0678 mutations in 2 to 8
percent of new MDR-TB diagnoses depending on cohort. MIC shift:
bedaquiline from 0.06 (S) to 0.25 to 1 (low-level resistance, often
under treatment-fail breakpoint of 0.25); clofazimine from 0.5 to 2 to 8;
bedaquiline-clofazimine cross-resistance is the practical concern.
Drugs NOT affected: pretomanid (Ddn-mediated activation pathway,
independent), linezolid (50S A-site, independent), moxifloxacin
(gyrA target, independent), older second-line drugs (ethionamide, PAS).
Diagnostics: Rv0678 sequencing on M. tuberculosis isolates with
treatment failure or relapse; phenotypic bedaquiline MIC; whole-genome
sequencing increasingly standard for MDR-TB workup. Implication:
emergent bedaquiline resistance during BPaL/BPaLM is a worrying
development; combination regimens minimize resistance emergence by
simultaneous multi-target attack; surveillance for Rv0678 mutations
essential during global rollout of new TB regimens.

response:
CTX-M-15 OVERVIEW.
CTX-M-15 = CEFOTAXIME-HYDROLYZING-MUNICH (the place where the first CTX-M was characterized). Class A serine β-lactamase. The DOMINANT ESBL GLOBALLY (≥80% of clinical ESBLs in many regions). Specifically efficient at hydrolyzing CEFOTAXIME + CEFTRIAXONE (the 'CTX' in the name).

MOLECULAR MECHANISM — STANDARD CLASS A SERINE β-LACTAMASE.
(1) 28 kDa monomeric protein, α/β fold.
(2) Active site: Ser70 (catalytic), Lys73, Ser130, Glu166, Lys234.
(3) Mechanism: Ser70 nucleophilic attack on β-lactam carbonyl → tetrahedral acyl-enzyme →     Glu166-activated water hydrolysis → opened-ring β-lactam released.
(4) DISTINCTIVE FEATURE: CTX-M's active-site Ω-loop is SHALLOWER than TEM/SHV (older ESBLs),     accommodating the BULKY METHOXYIMINO + AMINOTHIAZOL acyl chains of cefotaxime/ceftriaxone     that older β-lactamases cannot hydrolyze well.

SUBSTRATE SPECTRUM.
CTX-M-15 efficiently hydrolyzes:
  - PENICILLINS: rapid
  - 1G-2G CEPHALOSPORINS: rapid
  - CEFOTAXIME, CEFTRIAXONE (3G): rapid (defining feature — catalytic efficiency 1000× higher     than older β-lactamases)
  - CEFTAZIDIME (3G): MODERATE (slower than cefotaxime — CTX-M-15 has lower activity on     ceftazidime due to the carboxypropyl-oxime side chain)
  - CEFEPIME (4G): MODERATE-RAPID
  - CARBAPENEMS: NOT HYDROLYZED (CTX-M-15 is not a carbapenemase)
  - MONOBACTAMS (aztreonam): hydrolyzed

EVOLUTIONARY ORIGIN — KLUYVERA.
CTX-M evolved from CHROMOSOMAL β-lactamases of KLUYVERA species (Kluyvera ascorbata, Kluyvera georgiana, Kluyvera cryocrescens) — environmental Enterobacterales found in water + soil. Kluyvera chromosomal β-lactamases have similar substrate spectrum but are NOT transferable.

ISEcp1 (insertion sequence) MOBILIZED CTX-M from Kluyvera chromosome onto PLASMIDS in the 1980s-1990s. ISEcp1-mediated 'one-step' transposition can capture downstream genes — CTX-M was captured + spread on plasmids globally.

ALL CURRENT CTX-M VARIANTS (CTX-M-1 through CTX-M-200+) are descended from Kluyvera ancestors:
  CTX-M-1, CTX-M-3, CTX-M-15: from K. ascorbata lineage
  CTX-M-2, CTX-M-9, CTX-M-14: from K. georgiana lineage
Different geographic clades + plasmid backbones.

CTX-M-15 GLOBAL EPIDEMIOLOGY.
CTX-M-15 is the SINGLE MOST PREVALENT ESBL variant globally:
  India: 60-90% of clinical ESBLs (very high).
  China: 50-80%.
  Europe: 50-80%.
  US: 30-60%.
  Latin America: variable.
OFTEN CO-LOCATED on plasmids with: aac(6')-Ib-cr (FQ + AG resistance), sul1 + dfrA (TMP-SMX resistance), qnrB (FQ resistance) → multi-drug-resistance phenotype.

  ST405 — community-associated.
  ST38 — varies by region.

(1) ESBL E. coli COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED UTI: ~10-20% of all uncomplicated UTI in many regions.     Empirical TMP-SMX or FQ no longer reliable.
(2) ESBL Klebsiella + Enterobacter HOSPITAL infections: serious — requires CARBAPENEM Rx.
(3) ESBL bloodstream infections: high mortality without prompt CARBAPENEM Rx.
(4) ESBL TREATMENT RESPONSE: classical β-lactams (penicillin, ampicillin, cefazolin,     ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, ceftazidime) all FAIL on CTX-M-15+ strains. CARBAPENEMS,     PIPERACILLIN-TAZOBACTAM (variable), AMOXICILLIN-CLAVULANATE (community CTX-M variants),     or NEW BLI-COMBOS work.

Concerns about driving CARBAPENEM RESISTANCE → 'CARBAPENEM-SPARING' strategies:
  - PIPERACILLIN-TAZOBACTAM (Zosyn) — works on most CTX-M-15+ strains BUT MERINO trial showed     INFERIOR mortality vs meropenem for ESBL bloodstream infection. Use carbapenem when     available.
  - CEFTOLOZANE-TAZOBACTAM (Zerbaxa) — designed for Pseudomonas; works on ESBL+ E. coli too.
  - CEFTRIAXONE-SULBACTAM (research) — sulbactam adds modest ESBL coverage.
  - FLUOROQUINOLONES — only when susceptible (often co-resistant in CTX-M-15+ strains).
  - FOSFOMYCIN (oral) — uncomplicated cystitis only.
  - NITROFURANTOIN (oral) — uncomplicated cystitis.

(1) For ESBL+ Enterobacterales coverage, Lysos should generate β-lactams with EXTENDED     AMINOTHIAZOL-OXIME acyl side chains (cefotaxime/ceftriaxone-class) PAIRED WITH BLIs.

A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis in this clinical picture is less

rapid-strep test and culture for higher Centor scores (3 to 4).

SAR comparison: Trimethoprim vs iclaprim — deeper hydrophobic pocket of bacterial DHFR
response:
Both bind bacterial dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) at the folate-binding
pocket, blocking conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate (the
single-carbon donor for thymidine synthesis). Trimethoprim has a 2,4-
diaminopyrimidine ring linked via methylene to a 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenyl
group. Iclaprim retains the 2,4-diaminopyrimidine but extends the linker
and replaces the trimethoxyphenyl with a propenyl-cyclopropyl-methyl-
phenoxy substitution that reaches deeper into a hydrophobic groove of
DHFR specifically present in S. aureus and S. pneumoniae (deeper than
in human DHFR, by structural superposition). Result: iclaprim retains
activity against trimethoprim-resistant S. aureus carrying acquired
F98Y mutation in DHFR (a known TMP-resistance mutation that raises TMP
Ki by 1000-fold while iclaprim Ki rises only 8-fold); MIC50 of iclaprim
against MRSA is 0.06 ug/mL (TMP greater than 32 in TMP-R strains),
against VRE 0.5. Selectivity for bacterial vs human DHFR: iclaprim has
~10,000-fold selectivity, similar to TMP. Spectrum: iclaprim narrower
than TMP (no Stenotrophomonas, no Shigella) — the deeper hydrophobic
reach is gram-positive-selective. Resistance: dfrA17 plasmid-borne
DHFR variant defeats both; sul1/sul2 (sulfonamide-DHPS R) does not affect
iclaprim (it does not require sulfa partner). Pharmacology: iclaprim is
weakly basic and parenteral-only; phase 3 ABSSSI noninferior to vancomycin
(Holland 2020). Lesson: extending the substrate-mimicking arm of a
DHFR inhibitor into a deeper pocket can rescue activity against acquired
target mutation — the "second binding pocket" rescue strategy.

SAR comparison: Fluconazole vs voriconazole — triazole heterocycle and CYP51 binding
response:
Both are triazole antifungals binding the heme iron of fungal lanosterol-
14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51A in molds, ERG11 in yeasts). Fluconazole has
two 1H-1,2,4-triazole rings linked by a propan-2-ol with a 2,4-difluorophenyl
group; voriconazole keeps one triazole and one fluoropyrimidine ring with
a chiral methyl on the central carbon. The fluoropyrimidine of voriconazole
reaches deeper into a hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the heme, picking up
hydrogen bonds with Phe228 and Tyr132 of CYP51A. Result: voriconazole has
anti-Aspergillus activity (MIC50 0.5 to 2 ug/mL) where fluconazole is
essentially inactive (MIC greater than 64); voriconazole also covers
Scedosporium, Fusarium, and dimorphic molds (Histoplasma, Coccidioides).
Yeast activity: both cover Candida albicans (fluconazole MIC 0.25, vori
0.06), but voriconazole adds C. krusei (intrinsically fluconazole-R)
and improves C. glabrata coverage. Pharmacology: voriconazole has nonlinear
CYP2C19-driven metabolism (genetic polymorphism — poor metabolizers have
AUC 4-fold higher than extensive metabolizers; ultra-rapid metabolizers
undertarget), requiring TDM (target trough 1 to 5.5 ug/mL); fluconazole has
first-order linear renal-cleared PK without TDM. Resistance: fluconazole
to ERG11 mutations (Y132F in C. albicans) and CDR1/CDR2 efflux upregulation;
voriconazole to CYP51A TR34/L98H tandem-repeat promoter mutation in
Aspergillus (environmental azole-driven). Lesson: changing one of the two
triazole rings in fluconazole to a fluoropyrimidine bought mold activity at
the cost of TDM-required dosing — the "tighter pocket" SAR strategy.
